utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Jordash, I was informed that there was a matter you would like to raise, and there was also a matter pending still from yesterday which, perhaps, you could then raise after the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That was the matter. There is two matters I wish to raise. One was time estimates for the Simatovic witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the second was just to give Your Honours information about our three remaining witnesses and their availability. In relation to the Simatovic witnesses, we estimate for DFS-001 one and a half hours of examination. DFS-009, two hours. DFS-013, one and a half hours. And DFS-017, two hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to the -- our three outstanding witnesses, DST-071 has indicated -- has indicated that he will not attend without a subpoena. We'll file that subpoena application today. He said he is most available in the second two weeks of January. DST-067, that's Brown, has indicated that he's most available in the second two weeks of February or March. And DST-061 has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Most available is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I should say for Mr. Brown he said he's not available until the second two weeks of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're now struggling with that for availability to perform, job availability. Now, I do understand that, of course, the -- that the Prosecution needs some time to prepare, but there is a kind of a duty if you have committed yourself to become a witness or an expert, and I've some concerns about this Court have to adapt its schedule to when the witness is most available. I hope you understand. I mean, Mr. Brown was not available to make an agreement or to talk with the NFI people for quite some time. And, I mean, this Chamber would like to proceed rather than to hear where somewhere in the future someone is available or most available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just want to put this on the record, because as matters stand now we'll have to -- we'll consider the matter and we'll try to fit it all in into the Court schedule, but there comes a moment where the Court says, That's the time when the witness is supposed to appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate that, Your Honour. All I would say on Mr. Brown's behalf is that he's he -- he regularly attends Court so has a number of competing court interests. But I accept and understand what Your Honours are saying, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, if you please past that message. Please proceed, Mr. -- I interrupted you, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: DST-061 has indicated that -- he's indicated that he's available at the end of March, which I know, again, is not going to be terribly pleasing to the Court, but that's -- that's what he's indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's important that witnesses are available before we deliver judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I would rather have these witnesses done and away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see your point. It's not a personal criticism to you, but it's a general comment on how matters are developing and how matters are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for the information. Then, Mr. Jordash, the Chamber was informed that although Mr. Stanisic doesn't feel too well today that he, nevertheless, decided that he -- that he'd rather be in court than to excuse himself. Mr. Stanisic, if there is at any point in time any need to suspend or to have a break, don't hesitate to ask us. Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just clarify some of the discussion that we had yesterday with respect to the Simatovic expert. We have not dealt directly with the Defence military expert, although we did speak about the experts generally. The Prosecution yesterday sent another e-mail to the Simatovic Defence regarding DFS-020, the military expert. And this is the third e-mail making the same request that we've been making since the 17th of November regarding documents and supporting materials. In summary, the e-mail requests an English translation of the proposed military report, which is 700 pages, so it's a very sizable document; the complete compilation of the underlying source materials and the translations; as well as if they are 65 ter exhibits or exhibits introduced in the record of this case, that that be indicated so that we can locate them. And we do note that this report contains over 1.600 footnotes in 700 pages. So it's a very sizable document. So that there is not any undue delay, the Prosecution would appreciate a prompt response to our request for these materials so that we can hopefully avoid involving the Court itself in obtaining these materials and avoid having to file another motion to compel this information. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Mr. Petrovic, have you, and I'm really not referring to any specific knowledge of the content, but 700 pages for a military report seems to be rather large, which immediately raises the issue of relevance of all the information contained in it, and it is 1.600 footnotes. Have you considered that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'd like to raise a number of issues. We've been thinking about this very carefully. And if I have understood this correctly, while waiting for the Chamber's -- we're waiting for the Chamber's instructions with regard to this matter. The last time we discussed the matter, I believe it was said that we would receive instructions from the Chamber. Perhaps there's something that I misunderstood, but I think that that is what was said. But even without your instructions, without knowing your position, we've been thinking about this carefully and we will come to a conclusion that should satisfy you, Your Honours, and my colleagues from the Prosecution. And the other thing that I wanted to say is that the expert report was submitted for translation at the beginning of August of last year. On a number of occasions we were promised that it would translated by certain deadlines. The last deadline we were told about was the end of last year. It wasn't translated by that time. We continue to make requests for the translation to be completed, and the last time we asked about when it would be completed it was said immediately after the end of last year. We were told that two parts have been translated and another two parts have been drafted. The translation will soon be completed. And at some time in mid-January we were told we would have the translation. As soon as we receive the translation, we will naturally forward copies of the translation to our colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware of, the underlying documentation, is that available in English as well? Or what percentage is available in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a significant part is available, but I couldn't provide you with any numbers without first checking this. I could first check this and then with your leave I could provide you with the relevant information in a few days' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter at this moment? If not, then could witness DFS-014 be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DFS-014. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony in December of last year is still binding, that is, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Mr. Groome will now continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: DFS-014, where we left off yesterday, I had indicated that I would like to discuss with you information that the State Security Service had about you, and I think to do that safely it's probably best that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So I'd ask that we do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that P2673 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: While that's being done: During your direct evidence, Mr. Petrovic showed you this document, P2673, and you said it was written in the Ijkavian dialect of Serbo-Croatian, and not the Ekavian. And for the purposes of ensuring an accurate record: "Ijkavian" begins with Ij and Ekavian begins with the letter E. Do you recall your evidence on this point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You gave evidence that the Ijkavian dialect is used in Croatia in the Knin area. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Where, according to your knowledge, is the Ekavian dialect used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Ekavian dialect is spoken in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, other witnesses have given evidence before this Tribunal about the regional dialects. Is it your evidence that you can distinguish between dialects used in written documents from the words that are used, that an Ijkavian -- a person from an Ijkavian area would use some words and a person from an Ekavian area would use other words? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I have a problem with interpretation. But when a person arrives at a place where the Ekavian dialect is spoken, and if that person uses it otherwise naturally, he or she would maintain his dialect. Only after some time having spent a number of years in a different area that person would be able and willing to switch to the other dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is, is that we all recognise it may sound different, but from -- is it your evidence that actually different words will be used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People use different words. Two speakers of two different dialects use their respective dialects and words but still they can understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you were, you, yourself, were drafting a document that was going to be read primarily by people who spoke Ekavian dialect, would you be able to write it in such a way that it would be in their -- recognisable in their dialect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were writing a document, I'd write it in my language, in my dialect. However, if I am taking notes on dictation from someone else, I would use the dialect of the person who is supposed to sign the document. That was the rule of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that you now, with the help of the usher, take a pen, and can you mark the words in this document that you indicated it identified to you as being written by a person of Ijkavian dialect?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it seems to me that there was another misinterpretation. Mr. Groome is asking for the witness to mark the Ekavian words, whereas the witness received interpretation to the effect that he should mark the Ijkavian words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- take care that there's no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want you to mark -- before you make any mark on the document, let's confirm that you understand the instruction. I'm asking you to mark the words of the -- on this document that you recognise as being used in the Ijkavian dialect, the language spoken in Croatia and Knin. Okay? That it's different than spoken in Serbia. Do you understand my instruction to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So please underline each of those words that you recognised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. I can't mark the right words. The pen is imprecise. I was trying to underline the word "smjestaj" in the third line from the bottom, but I'm unable to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you do your best, and I will ask you to say each word afterwards so that we are sure that we have an accurate record of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've underlined eight different words. To ensure that we have an accurate record of your evidence, can I ask you to do the following: Can you go through each word, mention the word as written, the word that you've underlined, and then tell us what would be the Ekavian equivalent, the word you would expect to see had it been written from someone from Serbia. So can you do the first one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first word is "odjeljenje." In the Ekavian dialect, it would be "odeljenje," without the first J. The second word is "slijedecem." In the Ekavian dialect, the I and J would be missing. The third word: "uspjesno." In the Ekavian dialect, the J would be missing; it would be "uspesno." Then the next: "dijelu." In the Ekavian it would be "delu." "Smjestaj" in the Ekavian would be without the J. Next we have the "odjeljenje" again. The seventh word again is "smjestaj," whereas in the Ekavian the J would be missing. Next: "obezbjedjenje." In the Ekavian, the first J would be missing. I think we have a total of eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct in understanding that the primary difference is that in eight words there is a J included for the he Ijkavian dialect that would not be found in the equivalent word in the Ekavian dialect; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask that the screenshot be saved as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the relevance of this. Could we have an explanation, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Relevance of the evidence. Perhaps the witness takes off his earphones. Could you please take off your earphones. I understand that you're testing the solidity of the conclusions drawn by the witness on the basis of this written text.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: A little bit different than that, Your Honour. If -- we can't scroll down now because we'd lose the markings, but it's signed by FS, and it's the Prosecution's case that it's Mr. Simatovic's signature. My understanding of what Mr. Petrovic was doing when he was saying that this was a different dialect than Mr. Simatovic, I imagine that he's going to argue that it's not probable that it's Mr. Simatovic's signature because it was written in the Ijkavian dialect. So I'm just exploring this with the witness so that the Chamber has all the information it needs to make the determination it will have to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Registrar, could you assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document P2673, marked by the witness, will receive Exhibit P3060, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, DFS-014, I want to move to a completely different topic. It's your evidence that you don't know who Arkan reported to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But what reports do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't mean physical reports. I mean who he was subordinated to, who his superior in whatever command structure he was involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do apologise for intervening, but I really think that the question ought to be clear. We listened to what the witness was saying yesterday and who he was subordinated to during a certain period of time. We heard about what the witness knew, what he didn't know. What does Mr. Groome have in mind? Reported to whom, when, where?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll withdraw the question because it's going to distract us from the real inquiry I want to make at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to explain one of your answers that you have at T15813. Your answer was a bit unresponsive to the question, so I will simply read your answer: "According to the Vance-Owen Plan, the Krajina was not supposed to have an army, so many soldiers changed and were renamed into the special units of the police." Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has heard other evidence that this involved changing the colour of vehicles, changing uniforms from military -- colours usually identified as military to the colour blue, usually identified with the police. Is that part of what you're referring to here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We're talking about the period 1992, June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this was an attempt to deceive international observers by changing the appearance of personnel so that they appeared as if they were police personnel; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the political decision was taken by President Martic and the Government of the SAO Krajina. But I do know that those forces from the JNA that were withdrawing at the time gave rise to a new structure. There were new police units, and these police units were our only defence against the Croatian forces at the time. I don't know whether this was a matter of bypassing a planning or not. I wasn't responsible for implementing the Vance-Owen Plan and so on and so forth. I don't know what the intention was. But I do know that those forces protected all of us who lived in Krajina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you've given some evidence about the special units of the police, the PJP. Was that police unit also one of the police units that incorporated military personnel into its ranks after the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that there were these PJP units. They were part of the Ministry of the Interior at the time, but in fact they took over from the JNA. They were in fact local people from the area. They were reservists or active duty members of the JNA. As the JNA was leaving, the same people put on different uniforms, were transferred to the Ministry of the Interior, and they were then members of the special police units. And they were different from the police units of the regular kind. And their responsibility was to keep the peace and investigate crime. They were responsible for protecting the borders of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The specific question that I'm seeking your answer on is: To your knowledge, was the PJP in part comprised of personnel that had formerly been military personnel prior to the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To an extent they were part of the army of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in December, at T15815, in reference to Arkan's arrival, you said that it was celebrated because "he introduced order." Do you recall giving that answer? "Yes" or "no" will do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I stand by that claim to this very day. And that is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your evidence that Arkan, at least in part, fulfilled a police function as well as whatever military activities he may have been involved in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His task was to organise checkpoints around Benkovac and Obrovac so that the local inhabitants and the local troops wouldn't move out. Because there was panic in 1993. And in my opinion and in the opinion of everyone else he carried out this task together with his unit very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I would like to focus on some more information regarding Captain Dragan. At T15818, you said that Captain Dragan wanted to have more and more camps like Alfa. Do you recall giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, transcript of this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise, Your Honours. Yes, in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then the number seems to be wrong. It is 15818 you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recall your evidence about Captain Dragan wanting to establish more camps? 1

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I know that he wanted to open up more camps but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is: How did you know that? Is that something Captain Dragan told you himself, or did you learn that from other sources?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard about this from him. He said that he had set up a camp and that it was his intention to establish other training camps. But even the one that he established was a camp that he soon left, and that was the end of the role he was playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did he tell you where he wanted to set up these camps; simply in the Krajina, or in other areas of the former Yugoslavia as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was to do this in the area of Krajina. And this concerned recruits who were in the entire Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to return to the topic yesterday with respect to co-ordination between the SVK and Captain Dragan in 1993. At page 46 of yesterday's transcript, you provided the following evidence in response to questions from the Stanisic Defence: "Q. So is this right, you learnt that the military, the army, was sending recruits to Captain Dragan; Is that correct or not? "A. --"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to you read you the whole passage. "A. That's correct. That's true. "Q. How do you know that? Who told you that? "A. I know that because some of the officers of the Serbian army, of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, were deployed in Captain Dragan's camp. What they tried to do was to set up a brigade. "Vojvoda," "duke," which [sic] would have been under the command ..." Do you recall giving that evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 6343 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, may we take a break, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Groome, quarter past 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break. And we resume at quarter to 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that 65 ter 6343 be brought to the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, this is a report of the SVK Main Staff security intelligence organ, dated the 24th of February, 1993, which was sent to the attention of the RSK Main Staff forward command post. The first sentence in this report states: "We have information that some soldiers are leaving the first combat lines on their own initiative, that is, without the approval of their superior commands, and are going to Captain Dragan's training centre in Bruska." In light of this information, do you still maintain that the SVK command deployed or sent their recruits to Captain Dragan for training at the Alfa centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by what I claimed. And in relation to this document, I can say that the training centre for recruits took over that role at a subsequent date, the role of training recruits. Initially, it was a training centre. That's what Captain Dragan called it. A training centre for the troops, not just recruits. So what happened, it's true. What the report says, it's true. Certain combatants went to see Captain Dragan because he was a character in their eyes, someone who was capable of organising units and someone who was capable of leading these combat operations better than officers. And he showed his capacities in 1991. And since certain phenomena had been noted, well, this was a month from the aggression on the Republic of the Serbian Krajina in 1993, and this is why later a decision was taken according to which individual soldiers from the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina could go over to Captain Dragan but with the authorisation of the command that they were leaving. This had to be done on the basis of an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, it appears from your answer that you agree. That at least at the time of this report in February 1993 there was a problem that soldiers were deserting their positions on the front line and going without a proper authorisation to Captain Dragan's training centre. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with the statement concerning desertion. Desertion means leaving or abandoning one's combat positions. This is not a matter of deserting. It's the matter -- it's a matter of leaving one formation and entering another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, your answer just said: "Desertion means leaving or abandoning one's combat positions." And, again, the first line says: "Some soldiers are leaving the first combat lines on their own initiative." Is that not, in fact, desertion even by your definition of the term?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you leave the command of one unit and are placed under the authority of another unit, and if the other unit is also an active participant in combat, well, then, it's not a matter of desertion. You could say that individual combatants left the front lines responsible for the protection of certain units, but they became part of other units engaged in combat action. So whether they were in this unit or that unit, what one can say is that they participated in combat as per establishment at the time of the engagement of the unit in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter 6343.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 6343 will receive number P3061, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness DFS-014, could you assist us in the last line of the first linear of this letter. We see a reference to the OB. Are you familiar with that abbreviation? Do you know what it stands for? You see that it says that only after the intervention of OB and command, the transport with the complete crew was -- or at least the transport was returned to the unit. Could you tell us what OB stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the intervention of the security squad or the operative squad. I think it was the security squad or the other one, that it seems to be a matter of the brigade security squad. The 92nd Benkovac one must be what they have in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you think it is appropriate, perhaps I could be of assistance in relation to this acronym. If not ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm looking at the other parties because it's usually not counsel gives evidence. But if you could assist us in understanding what the acronym stands for, then I take it that there's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no objection since the witness has already given his evidence about what he thinks it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it is the security organ that it stands for. OB, I believe, stands for the "security organ."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that in the original language it is two words, the one starting with an O, the other one with a B. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: DFS-014, you've made several references to Captain Dragan somewhat unexpectedly disappearing from the Alfa Training Centre. Am I correct that he was there for approximately six months after he arrived and then he disappeared, as you characterised it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I remember exactly how long he was there for. I only remember his arrival and a very prominent event at the time. As I have already said, Bogunovic, the brigade commander, was killed. And so for a certain period of time this position was vacant. And I remember that Captain Dragan wanted to become the commander of the brigade of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and he had the support of certain soldiers whom he knew. But Colonel Dilas didn't allow this to happen, and he was prevented from becoming the head of that brigade, so he then left Krajina. And as I have already said, the camp was part of the 7th Corps under the command of the Colonel Dilas. So I don't know whether it was after six month or after five months, but he did disappear and left Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that the Alfa Training Centre in Bruska was not placed under the command of the Army of Republic of Serb Krajina until the 25th of June, 1993? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And just for the Chamber's benefit, that was a reference to D71, an exhibit introduced by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: For my next series of questions I think that it is best that we go into private session to ensure that we do not compromise your identity. And if I could that we do that now. And I will conclude my examination after these next few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Any need for further questions? Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll be now further cross-examined by Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I, before I begin, Your Honour, just to clarify with the Prosecution a certain issue. I have a document which I was going to use to establish a certain fact about the Alfa training camp, but I don't need to use it if the Prosecution confirm something which they appeared to suggest a moment ago, which is that they accept that the Alfa Training Centre was under the command of the Army of the RSK at least from the 25th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would need some time to review all of the evidence on the point. I'm not prepared off the top of my head to make a binding agreement on a fact. I'd ask to take a look at the document. I'm not even sure what document Mr. Jordash is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it's more that Mr. Groome put to the witness: "Are you aware that the Alfa Training Centre was placed under the command of the Army of the RSK by 25th of June, 1993?" Which seemed like a positive assertion to me. But if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, D71 says that the 107th training centre for reconnaissance and sabotage activity with a postcode in peacetime at the Main Staff of the SVK command was established by the order of the SVK commander, which of course leaves open what was the situation before that, whether there was no Alfa training camp or whether it was under a different authority. So I think the best thing would be, Mr. Jordash, that you present the evidence you would like to present and ask questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. Could I have then -- Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jordash:

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just want you, Mr. Witness, to have a look at a document and see if you can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05292, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you just take a moment to read that page and then read the second page so that you've got a full picture of what it says.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And let's have a look at the next page so you've got the full picture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And can we go to the second page, please, of the B/C/S and also the English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read this, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp that we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's the stamp of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Krajina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just have a moment to formulate a view? I'm just trying to get some more information about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then let's then mark it for identification at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5292 will receive number P -- D618 [Realtime transcript read in error "168"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. May we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- page 10 of the English and 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And it's -- if you go to line 18, Mr. Witness, and read from the words "from 12th of October, 1991," down to the words "Second Administration." Sorry, it's line 11 for you down to line 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, shouldn't the witness have the benefit of knowing what this is and who it is that's speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I thought it was fairer to the witness, so I didn't lead him and could -- to leave it as open as possible so the witness could say one way or another without understanding who said it. But I'm in Your Honours' hands. If the Prosecution thinks it's fairer, then I'm happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To start with, you can put your question as you did, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Have you read that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it's the Prosecution case, as I understand it, that that paragraph reflects the truth; that the Serbian DB had both a unit command and an intelligence team from the Second Administration who were effectively co-ordinating 5.000 soldiers in battles in those locations. Would you have known if that was the case? Would you have expected to hear about that, whether formally or informally, from the position you were in in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether I should have known, it's something I'm not certain of in 1991. But in 1991 and 1992 I took part in combat and was later at the location I specified. And in such positions I probably would have heard of some such statements as this one, and I may have been in a position to know some details, but I didn't. I am unaware of what is referred to in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The reality is, isn't it, Mr. Witness, that if there'd been a unit command operated by the Serbian DB co-ordinating battles in Benkovac in 1992 you surely would have known about it or heard something about it, no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the time I wasn't there, I probably would have learned something about it from the stories that went around, but I never heard that someone from the Serbian DB co-ordinated some activities or clashes in the area of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Let's just move on to one other aspect and then I'll be able to finish my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we go to page 11 of the English and 8 -- and stay at 8 of the B/C/S. And I'm looking for where it -- where the text discusses 26 training camps for special police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I think it's at line 25 for you down to line 30.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Am I correct that Obrovac and Gracac and Benkovac are three locations very close to each, other within several kilometres; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are close. Perhaps not by a few kilometres but a few dozen kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's the Prosecution case that the Serbian DB set up, organised, supplied, had instructors positioned within camps, training camps in Obrovac, Gracac, Benkovac, would you have expected to know about that or hear something about that or see something about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to comment on this statement starting from line 25, I could say the following: As far as I know, I knew of the training centre in Golubic. When they refer to Dinara, which is a mountain, it's something I don't know what they have in mind exactly. It's uninhabited and there had been a tank firing range before there, the so-called "crvena zemlja [phoen]," but there were no facilities there or anything else. There was nothing in Obrovac either as far as I know because I visited it later on in 1993, 1994, and 1995. There was no training centre there. As for Gracac, as far as I know from conversations with the police personnel in Gracac, there was nothing there. As for Benkovac, I know for sure that there was no centre. When I was there I would have been aware of such a centre, but it wasn't there when I was there. Unless we are discussing Bruska. There was no other training centre for the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you very much for your very complete answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about the rest of the area. I'm not familiar with Plitvice, Samarice, or let alone Banja Luka and Republika Srpska. There's nothing I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Petrovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- asks his questions, I had asked for a moment to do a -- consider a view on D168 [sic]. The Prosecution has no objection to the admission of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D168 [sic] is admitted into evidence. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry for standing up again, but I was referring to the transcript. Apparently, we believe, the transcript incorrectly recorded the exhibit, but it's the last exhibit that Mr. Jordash sought to tender. I'll leave myself in the hands of the Court Officer to identify the correct exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the shooting, the shooting exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's the document that was marked for identification pending --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And it was the exhibit that contained the stamp. And as you asked, Mr. Jordash, "Is this the stamp of the Army of the Serbian Republic of the Krajina?" But it even is more detailed because the stamp itself refers to the Alfa Training Centre as apparently a part of that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Madam Registrar, that was -- the last one was D168? It was marked for identification. I have to check that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's D618, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 618, yes. 168 seemed to me to be a very low number. D618 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Witness. First I would like to put some questions to you about what we have heard today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 2D270, item 2. 2D270.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a report from the command of the 7th Corps of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It's dated the 2nd of March, 1993. Please have a look at the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the benefit of the Chamber, could you please display the translation 2D270, and it's the very same document. If we could show both versions at the same time. We do have the translation. It was uploaded -- a copy from the book was uploaded and then we received a copy from the Republic of Croatia -- or, rather, we received the original documents from the Republic of Croatia at a somewhat later date. Your Honours, it's the last paragraph on the page that you can now see on your screens. It's a report from the 7th Corps command. And it says that the intervention platoon, the Lisica Group, went to carry out a combat task of reconnaissance under the command of Captain Dragan in the Biljane Donje and Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, does this show that Captain Dragan received orders from the command of the 7th Corps? And you in fact testified to that effect before this Court.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see from this document that Captain Dragan received orders from the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and this report from the command of the 7th Corps that is addressed to all the units involved in combat in the area of Benkovac -- well, you can see that they were sent this report so they could be informed. This shows that he received orders from the command of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, whether it was the command in Benkovac which was a temporary command at a forward command post but was in fact the command of the 7th Corps of the Serbian army of Krajina, well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in the same paragraph it continues and says: "The Alfa Training Centre from where this reconnaissance group is carrying out its tasks according to plan," how do you take this? What -- whose plan do they have in mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably means the plan of the Alfa Training Centre. It's probably the plan that they draft and is then authorised by the high command so that the plan could be carried out. So it was for the high command, the command of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, to provide authorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Petrovic. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript: Witness, which command is the one that would authorise the plans of the Alfa Training Centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was certainly the 7th Corps of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be tendered into evidence on behalf of the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, first of all it should be clarified, because there are three documents apparently, and you told us that apart from the version in the book that there was now a translation available; although, it seems that the English version you've shown to us is now still from the book, isn't it? Because the translation refers to footnotes, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. This is the problem that we have encountered on a number of occasions. It's identical, but the layout of the text is somewhat different. But the essence, the substance of the report has been correctly translated and corresponds to what we can see in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and has been translated by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] CLSS, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I invite the parties to agree on the accuracy of the substance and that we ignore whatever is there which does not reflect the English translation of the document alone, and ignore any reference to or any text which is taken from the book rather than from the document itself. Yes. Madam Registrar, would you then know what document to use? Or ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I would like now have a clarification if the tendered document is 2D270.2 or 2D270.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The original is 2D270.2 and the translation is 2D270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I invite you, Mr. Petrovic, to consult with Madam Registrar during the next break and then we'll put the matter on the record once it is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to remind the Chamber about its original ruling with response -- in regards this reoccurring problem. It is the Prosecution's understanding that they would be -- all these documents would be MFI'd when the translations are verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the translation is correct. We have checked it. As I have said, it's just the layout that is at stake. We have footnotes, for example, that state who is who. We could neglect this or we could -- we don't want to create more problems, more confusion. But the translation of the text is adequate and it has been professionally done. We could go into other details and examine the matter, but we would be wasting resources unnecessarily if we did so, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original document, which is 2D270.2, is that -- Madam Registrar, is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, may I just clarify for everyone what the problem is. We have two documents, one is 2D20 -- 2D270, which has English and B/C/S version, and the other one is 2D270.2, which has just the correct B/C/S version. From the Registry point we can assign a number only to one document, one quoted document, not to two of them. Or we can assign separate numbers. So if the party can compile one document with a number to be assigned to it, then we can assign number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please -- would you please do so. Apparently for Madam Registrar now the major problem is not the translation itself but that the translation contains also a different B/C/S version. Is that ... because there are two documents, both an original, and we are not going to spend further time on this in court. Please consult with Madam Registrar during the break and then we'll finally assign a number and decide on admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. Thank you. We have the same situation with the following document that I will show the witness. Could we please show the following document: 2D273.2. And the translation, the English version of the document: 2D273.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down in the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And please, witness, have a look at item number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you scroll down a little bit more -- or, in fact, could we see the second page in the B/C/S version. I believe that we have a different document in the B/C/S version. 2D273.2, the second page. In the English we have the right part. And could the Chamber please have a look at the second paragraph in item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the first paragraph that you have in front of you. Witness, have you had a look at it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What you can see here, would you say that it corresponds to your testimony according to which the Alfa Training Centre reported to the corps command on the training that was being provided there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what this seems to show.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The beginning of counsel's question was missed. Could counsel please repeat the question with the microphone on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question with the microphone on. And then also, Mr. Petrovic, to ask, "Does this document show this and this and this?" is all rather vague. Could you please focus on the text of these kind of documents and ask exactly what justifies the kind of conclusions you are ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, it says training in the Alfa camp is settling into a routine even though there have been problems with materiel provisions. Strict military disciplinary measures are being implemented, and all those who fail to adhere to them are being dismissed from the training centre. My question is as follows: Does what is stated in the document correspond with the information you have in relation to the corps command and the training centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This portrays the situation that I have already described or such as I have already described it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does what is stated in the document correspond to the information you have according to the corps command and the training centre. I mean, Mr. Petrovic, could you be more precise. What does it then, as you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the translation, the interpretation, is not correct. I asked whether this corresponded with the information the witness has on the relations between the centre and the corps command, or does he have information of a different kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What it says here in this document is that the training in the Alfa center is slowly settling into a routine even though there have been problems with material provisions. "Strict military disciplinary measures are being implemented and all those who fail to adhere to them are being dismissed from the training centre." What does that say at all apart from that it describes a situation in a training centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to seek this document to support or confirm what the witness knows about a relation, then it should be clear, first of all, what the witness tells us exactly about that relation; and then second, to what extent the text of this document provides support. And the questions are so general that I have difficulties in establishing what you, apparently, seek to establish on the basis of the testimony of the witness and this document. Could you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we are talking about information to subordinate units provided by the 7th Corps command. And in this information, or the report, information is provided according to which what certain units or institutions do under the corps command, and their activities on the 13th of May, 1993, are also described. Witness, does the document clearly show what you have testified about; namely, that the Alfa Training Centre as part of the ARSK was under the command of the 7th Corps of the ARSK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the report was provided to the units that was under this command. The report won't be sent to someone else. If you don't send a report to the high command -- well, they would compile a collective report for the entire 7th Corps command and then they would send it to the other units so that all the other units could be familiar with the situation. In other units they would describe the situation such as it was in the entire corps. And all the units from the corps were to be informed of that situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document also be admitted into evidence. But I believe that we have to agree on this with the Registry as was the case with the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'll do, I'll ask Madam Registrar to reserve a number for the previous document and this one so once the issue with the various B/C/S and English versions has been resolved that at least we have reserved numbers for them. The previous one would be, Madam Registrar ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document 2D270.2, or not, will receive number D619, reserved. And document 2D273.2, or not, will receive number D2 -- D620 reserved, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Could the witness take off his earphones for a second. Mr. Petrovic, I'll explain to you what my problem is. Paragraph 2 of this document describes in the first part what happened during fighting, units of the Serbian army had no dead or wounded soldiers, and then at a certain moment it says: "The training in the Alfa Training Centre is slowly settling into a routine ..." So then it continues with the training centre. Now, the core issue is whether that means that the Alfa Training Centre was -- one of the unit was subordinated; or whether, after having described what our units have done, that it then described what the Alfa Training Centre does or does not. That's the issue. Now, what you do is you put to the witness, "Doesn't it clearly show this and this and this?" Now, whatever the witness says, it needs a careful analysis of the text to understand whether this is a conclusion you could draw from this document. And it is of no use to go over it by a quick question and a quick answer. Reading it, two interpretations are possible. Now, of course, the issue then is: What would be the reason to adopt the one interpretation and what would be good reasons to adopt the other interpretation? The one is "our units, including the Alfa centre as a training centre for our units." The other one is "our units and, apart from that, the alfa centre." Now, that's the issue which the Chamber has to consider. Again, to ask a witness and say, "Doesn't it show clearly that one," the witness says yes or the witness says no -- what we need is good reasons to adopt either the one or the other interpretation of this document. Of course, the Chamber finally will have to consider the whole matter in the context of the entirety of the evidence. But even for this document it may be relevant to find out why the witness adopts the one interpretation, whether he has any reasons apart from the text of the document, because the text of the document seems to be ambiguous. I just explain this to you in order to make you aware of what the Chamber needs, what kind of questions should be put to witnesses, and what the Chamber needs in order to evaluate the answers. And just saying, "This is what the document seems to say," is, of course, not a very solid basis for making any findings for this Chamber. Would you please keep this in mind and we'll ask the witness to put his earphones on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One second, witness. Witness DFS-014, could you take them off again. I'm sorry. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just explain my position. Witness made a clear statement here that his personal experience is that Alfa was under the command, under the subordination, of the 7th Corps. That is his evidence before the Chamber. I just wanted to show the documents which corroborates his position and ask him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly the matter. Whether this document corroborates or does not corroborate his position. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, I do understand that. But I just wanted to show that -- to try to extract a bit more information from his knowledge when I present these documents to him. That was my intention, and I will try to -- I will try to put questions which will be more beneficial to the Chamber as you instructed me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the witness can put his earphones on again. Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness be shown 2D266.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is D617 -- [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D266 in English. And 2D266.2 is the original in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, have a look at the document, please. It is a 7th Corps command report, dated the 12th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go down the page, please, so that the witness can see the last paragraph. In the English version we should go to page 2 for the benefit of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This information was sent to the subordinate units. And the paragraph I am interested in reads as follows: "Quartermaster supplies arrived, were received and distributed yesterday. The newly arrived squad and platoon commanders were transferred to the Alfa Training Centre for training." Witness, the Prosecutor suggested that the Alfa Training Centre was part of the ARSK as of end of June 1993. Do you know whether as of the moment the centre was established people, recruits, were sent there who came from the ARSK ranks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, once the training centre Alfa was established, which was also equipped in haste with the necessary accommodation facilities and the rest, soldiers began arriving immediately, as we could see in the -- in one of the previous documents where the security organ was informing that the soldiers were leaving their units and moving to Captain Dragan to the Alfa Training Centre. Since the situation was tense at the time and there was daily combat and shelling not only at the front lines but in the rear as well, in Benkovac and other settlements, and civilians were being killed, only once the situation stabilised along the front lines did recruits start attending training in the training centre called Alfa. It may have been in February or March. In any case, I assert that the training centre Alfa was always under the command of the ARSK. At the outset it was under the command of Benkovac, when people and equipment were being sent there. Later on, as the training centre and the place where the Vojvoda Vuk unit were supposed to be established fell under the army directly and not under the Benkovac unit. It was simply put directly under the command of the 7th Corps, that's the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we reserve a number for this document?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honours, this document was MFI'd on 15th of December last year as D617, but only the document 2D00266.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to fully understand the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am also trying to understand what exactly the document says. I mean, it's clear what the testimony of the witness is, is that the Alfa Training Centre was on from the beginning part of the Army of the Serbian Krajina, but I am just wondering and asking myself what this document gives in support. You quoted "quartermasters supplies arrived, were received and distributed. Yesterday the newly arrived squad and platoon commanders were transferred to the Alfa Training Centre for training." Witness DFS-014, could you explain to us to what extent the lines quoted by Mr. Petrovic support your view that the training centre was a unit within the structure of the Army of the Serbian Krajina at the time of this document, that is, in, I think it's March 1993. It says that "... newly arrived squad and platoon commanders were transferred to the Alfa Training Centre for training." What does that say about the Alfa Training Centre being part of the military structure I just referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a military document. It contains reports which had to do with the army, the 7th Corps specifically. As we see, there is no mention here of any members of the MUP of the Serbian Krajina; that is to say, of my station and my superior command in Knin which, at the same time, had its forces deployed along a part of the front lines in Pridrag [phoen], near Karin, Benkovac municipality. We can see in the document that there is no reference to that unit at all. Only such units are mentioned that the army is responsible for. There is no mention made of any police units, of civilians, and whether any civilians were killed or not. This is a purely military document. If it refers to the Tactical Group 4 or to a brigade or a unit, when they mention Alfa it is understood that it too is a military unit. You see that there are no MUP units mentioned there despite the fact that they were at the front lines at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what you say is, "It's my understanding that sending people to the Alfa Training Centre implicitly means that the Alfa Training Centre is part of our military structure"? That's what you're telling us, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is what I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's not an explicit reference but it is for you an implicit reference. That's clear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let us go back to this document, the paragraph above this one. It reads: "Due to people who were not qualified to man the TG-4 asset, one fighter was killed and another injured in the unit of Captain Dragan in the past 24 hours." How do you interpret this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I conclude from this that the unit of Captain Dragan was part of the army. If in the same paragraph we have a mention of his, within this one-sentence paragraph, this is what it means to me. They are basically saying that they had people who were not qualified to man a recoilless gun and as a result one of them was killed and another injured. And in Captain Dragan's units, two fighters were wounded in the past 24 hours. To me it means that it is one in the same military formation and is portrayed as such in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then -- a follow-up question, Mr. Petrovic. Could you tell us -- this is a report to the subordinated units. Now, we see that the soldier being injured due to improper handling of a recoilless gun is a TG-4 soldier. Now we see that Tactical Group 4 is specifically mentioned as the part of the 92nd Motorised Brigade, Operations Group 1. Now, where do I have to put Captain Dragan's unit in the addressees of this document, which is a report to subordinated units? Where? Is it part of the 75th or is it part of the 1st Light Brigade? Where is Captain Dragan's present in the addressees of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, in March, I would put it under the 22nd Motorised Brigade, in that category. It's the Benkovac Brigade, and he actually belonged to it. He received equipment from them as well as ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, that seems to be interesting, because the report where it tells us about the soldier from TG-4, we see that that unit is specifically mentioned, TG-4, as a sub-unit of the 92nd Motorised Brigade. However, where do I find as a specific subordinated unit Captain Dragan's unit? Because if you say a soldier from the 4th Tactical Group was injured and a soldier of Captain Dragan's unit or two soldiers were wounded, then I would -- where the address to the units, the subordinated units, is so specific in relation to Tactical Group 4, why doesn't it say anything about Captain Dragan's unit? Which, as you told us, you assumed was part of the 92nd Motorised Brigade. Why doesn't it say "4th Tactical Group, Captain Dragan's unit"? Could you explain that? Do you have any knowledge of it? If you don't know, then please tell us as well. But I'm just trying to analyse the document, what I see in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, upon arriving in Benkovac, well, Captain Dragan went there on a voluntary basis, so as far as I know he wasn't ordered to go there by the military hierarchy. He didn't arrive with documents which would place him within a certain unit. He arrived, he was given a facility, he started equipping it in terms of logistics, for accommodation. He organised the kitchen. He would receive certain equipment, beds, and so on and so forth, things that he obtained from the French Battalion camp, from the Karin place, because on the 23rd of January I think that camp was shelled by the Croatian army and three French soldiers were killed who were fleeing, and later he took equipment from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a moment. What apparently you are explaining to us is that in terms of equipment Captain Dragan's unit, who arrived as a volunteers unit, that he was facilitated in the way you describe. Now, I'm less interested in this moment, perhaps to some extent but not primarily interested, in where the beds came from and whether it came from a French unit or from an English unit or from whoever. I'm interested in subordination. Could you continue your answer. But then specifically in relation to subordination, that is, who gives orders, who reports to whom, military hierarchy, could you explain why Captain Dragan's unit is not mentioned in any way among the addressees, although the report tells us something about his casualties or at least injuries in his unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you that at the time when the Croatian army first launched its attack there was no time nor was there any desire to discuss certain administrative issues. It was necessary to rapidly adapt to the situation. At such a time when you are short of men and when you are fighting for each position, when 20 soldiers die on a daily basis, in such a situation you haven't got time to see who agrees with what and how to do certain things. You improvise. People arrive, you say there's ammunition here or there. Then someone tells you that there's a company or platoon that's available. You send them to positions. You provide ammunition. Later many things are co-ordinated as necessary, but at the time the people who are gathered there had to be sent to the front line. And it was important for them to contribute to the defence of the Serbian people at that time and in that area, and that's why I said from the outset he was with the Benkovac unit. And it is there that he received combat ammunition and other things. People gradually moved over to his side from other units. He didn't appear with his own unit. He came there as an individual. He arrived there on his own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But with his own men? Or not? Did he come with a unit or did he come just on his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He arrived on his own. He was alone. And then on the basis of his former acquaintances he obtained men. People went over to his side. The people, the soldiers -- or the army had problems because men would leave units and join up with him, because there was an myth according to which he was a superman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, what you describe, and please correct me when I'm wrong, what you describe is a situation where there's no clear hierarchical military structure in which Captain Dragan can be placed, but, rather, that people were in combat side by side having the same aim on their mind rather than formally structured in a hierarchical situation, at least at the beginning of the time. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a formal hierarchical structure based on the units that were in the field at the time of the attack in the area. But when Captain Dragan arrived, he formed on his own initiative a unit which immediately joined the combat. And later the training centre was transformed and that's why he later became part of the corps structure and belonged to the corps. You know, I was in the area. When things are okay, everyone says it's due to their own qualities. That was also the case with the captain. When it was necessary to use him in combat, they would say that he was part of this corps or brigade; but if they didn't need him, they said, "He is not one of ours, you deal with him and solve the situation." So it was a sort of -- the Benkovac Brigade and the 7th Corps kept sending the ball into the other camp, into each other's camp, and the commander of the brigade died at that time, about 20 days prior to that time, so you can see what the situation was like then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed two parts of your answer, and let's just verify whether that's what you said and what you intended to say. That Captain Dragan arrived, he formed on his own initiative a unit which immediately joined combat, and later the training centre was transformed and that he later became part of the corps structure. Which means that in the beginning, when he formed his unit, he was not yet part of the corps structure. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You haven't understood me correctly. Perhaps the interpretation was incorrect. He appeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say the interpretation is wrong, we'll check that. Please be aware of that, that we'll ask again to -- that your original words will be listened to and that we'll verify whether the translation is correct or not. So therefore, I urge you to tell us, what I just read to you, whether that is what you said and whether that is what you intended to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Captain Dragan arrived on his own in Benkovac. He appeared. They called me to the barracks. We then -- or, rather, the municipality assigned him a facility in Bruska and immediately certain combatants started leaving their units and joined Captain Dragan's unit. And he used these men to form a unit with which he joined in the combat operations under the command of the Benkovac Brigade. Then many units from the Krajina came to assist, as ordered by the army commander, and he participated in the combat as did the other units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this formalised in any way, that they were still acting under the command of the Benkovac Brigade? Is there any document, is there any decision?
