Because it's a funny kind of military hierarchy where people are leaving their units going to someone else who has no formal position then join him and everyone joins in combat, and that's all under the umbrella of the Benkovac Brigade who has not, as I understand, has not ordered Captain Dragan to form such a unit, who has never ordered soldiers to go from there own unit to Captain Dragan's unit, especially because you also said - and that was the second part of your answer I would like to verify - is that you said, "When it was necessary to use him in combat, they would say he was part of this corps or brigade; but if they didn't need him, they said that he's not one of us." That means that it's a rather vague situation where the military hierarchy is not, at least, firmly established, because it depends on what they say today and depends on what they say tomorrow. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would agree with that, with what you have said. That was the situation which was the result of the confusion in the field. When the commander of the brigade was killed and his position was vacant, I said that Captain Dragan then had the ambition to become the commander of that brigade, and he launched certain attacks with his -- or, rather, wanted his men, some of his men, to support that. But when the corps command and Commander Dilas reacted and refused to appoint him to the position of the brigade commander, the situation was resolved. It was only later that he became an integral part of the corps, which you can see in some of the documents that I have been shown here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, whether we can see it or not is -- needs further evaluation. I apologise for having a very late break. We'll take a break. And we resume at five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be shown 2D157.2. The English is 2D157, or, rather, the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, the document before us is from the command of the 1st Operative Group. The barracks of Benkovac is the command place. It says: "Order for further action." The date is the 4th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the second page in the Serbian version and in the English. Could we see the second page in the other version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, under item 5 in this order, orders are issued for further activities. It says: "The Vukovi Battalion on Stosija-Glavina axis shall attack in the direction of the village of Rezani and must break up the Ustasha in the village of Krasici [phoen], near the church." It says the Vukovi Battalion; do you know who this refers to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Vukovi from Vucjak. Veljko Milankovic's Vukovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where is the unit from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's from the place called Prnjavor in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone please]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the following paragraph, where it says: "The Tiger Battalion shall launch an attack on the Perica-Glava village of Palja [phoen] axis, and its task shall be to break up the Ustashas in the village in the Paljuv [phoen] and in co-ordination with the CMKMN it shall continue with the attack in the direction of Novi Grad. Witness, who does this refer to, the "Tiger Battalion"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan's unit, which was called the "Tigers." And when it says to co-ordinate that with the company of the police from Knin, CMKMN, refers to this company from Knin because at the time we held this area from Pridraga and Palja in the direction of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the bottom of the document on the left-hand side. Could you tell us who these documents were forwarded to? What do these markings mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here it says forwarded to the command of the 7th Corps, to the 92nd Brigade, to the command of the Banja Brigade, to the command of the Kordun Brigade, to the command of the Vukovi Battalion, in fact, B means battalion, so it's the Banja Battalion, also to the command of the 92nd Armoured Brigade, and also to the archives. And it also says command -- the commander, the Colonel Tanga. He was the deputy of -- Djilas's deputy. He was the chief of the 7th Corps staff and the commander of Operative Group 1 which was subsequently moved from the barracks to the Biljane Gornje place, and the command was there for a long time. And it was also forwarded to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Witness, yesterday in answer to a question by my colleague Mr. Groome you could that written orders were issued to all the units that were part of the Serbian army of Krajina and that participated in these combat operations. Is this one such order that you had in mind when you were answering my colleague Mr. Groome's questions yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that according to the rules the army had to act in this manner, and this is an example of how it was to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could this document please be marked for identification at this point in time, because the document has a similar status as the previous one that we have already discussed today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could a number be reserved, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The reserve number for 2D157.2 or 2D157 would be D621, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question for the witness: Have you any knowledge as where the Vukovi or the Tiger Battalion was placed in the military hierarchy? It was subordinated to whom or to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of the Tiger Battalion and the command of the Vukovi Battalion were subordinated to the military command. When they arrived, they reported to the military command and continued working in concerted action with the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but was there any -- any subordination to another unit or to ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their immediate superior command was the 7th Corps. They were subordinated to the command of the 7th Corps in co-ordination with the other units in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this a direct command structure, then? Did they receive their orders directly from the corps command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As we can see here, we have a Banija Battalion and a Kordun Battalion. These comprised regular members of the army from the area of Banija and Kordun. Due to the war, they were transferred to the area of Dalmatia, near Benkovac, and they served the same function as the Vukovi and Tigers battalions. They all came there on orders. They were subordinated to the corps commander and then he tasked the commander of the operative group Colonel Tanga to be in charge. He acted as deputy corps commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still not an answer to my question. My question is: From whom did the command of the Vukovi Battalion and the Tigrovi Battalion receive their orders? Who said, "Now you should do this, now you should do that"? Was that from the corps command or was that from any lower command? If you know -- if you don't know, then, of course, you can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have said: When I attended two meetings in the command room when commander Bogunovic was still alive, they received orders from him. He was a local and his unit was the biggest one, the 92nd Brigade. It was between six and a half and 7.000 men strong. It was the largest motorised brigade in the Knin corps. They had their own armoured battalion and artillery. It was a full brigade. At the time they received their orders from him. Now, how it was structured in legal terms and in terms of structure is something I don't know. I guess they followed military rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, in the document which is before us, we see that reference is made, for example: "The main forces shall co-ordinate actions with a battalion of the 92nd Motorised Brigade and the Vukovi Battalion to take control of," et cetera. That language suggests that the Vukovi Battalion is not integrated or subordinated to the 92nd Motorised Brigade. And we find that not only once, but we find similar language a bit further down as well. At the second part of the document it says: "A Battalion of the 92nd Motorised Brigade shall attack," et cetera, et cetera, "and strike the flank with artillery support and in co-ordination with the Banija Battalion and the Vukovi Battalion," which also suggests that these battalions are not subordinated to the 92nd Motorised Brigade. Do you have any comment on the language used in view of what I just said? Any comment on the language used in this document? Because you explained to us that you heard orders being issued by the command of the 92nd Motorised Brigade to these battalions when you were present during those meetings, whereas the language here could be interpreted in a different direction as well. Do you have any comments on the language used here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unit structures were set up before that. We -- it was known that the brigade had four infantry battalions, and so on and so forth. This was the regular structure as it existed before the attack. Since the attack came out of the blue and the units were sent there to support and assist in attempts to regain territory, the structure was not changed per se, so to have the battalions strictly under the command of the brigade. But it was well understood who commanded. At the time, on the spot, there were officers from the superior command, that is to say, from the corps command and the Main Staff; they jointly analysed the situation and issued orders. We have a situation here in which the deputy corps commander issued such an order. At the time the Benkovac Brigade was the largest brigade and the commanding officer was the person who knew the situation best, and it was normal that he provided suggestions and then the superior commander could accept his proposals and translate them into written orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the orders were given by the deputy corps commander, that is, Colonel Tanga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was there, too, as far as I remember. He commanded Operative Group 1, which served as the forward command post of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've -- I was asking myself, where you refer to the deputy commander, that this order seems to have been issued by the commander of the 1st Operational Group, is that -- that is below the corps level but above the brigade level, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm trying to understand what exactly the hierarchical structures were at the time. Mr. Petrovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Perhaps to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Operational Group, what was it part of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 7th Knin Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Dragan Tanga was deputy corps commander who at the same time performed the duties of commander of the 1st Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was deputy corps commander and in this case he figures as deputy corps commander because there was combat in his area. The corps commander was responsible for the entire corps area, from Obrovac to Vrlika, and his deputy had a remit which was more narrow in terms of territory so that he would be better prepared for action in a limited area. That is why the operational group was established and that is how he became commander of that operational group as his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the document entitled "Order for Further Action," in item 5 we read: "The Tiger Battalion is to attack along the axis of Perica-Glava." How do you understand this sentence? Who issued orders to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I see it, the commander of the operational group, Colonel Tanga, issued an order to the Tiger Battalion, to its command, to attack along that axis as specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session for the next few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The objection is denied. The words "operational group" and "tactical group" have been used, and Mr. Groome is in a position to verify with the witness whether his understanding, in the understanding of the witness, is correct or not. If not, then we might have to turn to expert evidence. Could you answer the question whether Mr. Groome did understand the words "tactical group" and "operational group" in a sense you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a tactical group and an operative group, well these are military terms that I didn't learn about in school. But as far as I have understood, or as far as I understood during the war that I lived through, there were certain things that I had to master. I had to adapt to the situation. But from what I learned, a tactical group and operative group are groups that are composed or formed for a certain area. They are a small command. We have a tactical group, an operative group, for example, in the Benkovac area that was subordinated to the corps command from Knin, and some representatives of the corps commander would be in charge of them, so it included a smaller number of units than the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can I just put -- I think we will proceed quicker if I can just put what I believe the definition is and if you can tell me whether I'm correct or I'm not correct. So it seems you would agree with me that it's put together for a particular area, at least; is that correct? An operational group or tactical group is especially created to deal with a special or a particular area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that a tactical group or operational group is made up of personnel from different units, perhaps different army units, perhaps different volunteer units, perhaps different police units. Am I correct in that understanding of a tactical group or operational group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say that you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, my next question to you is: At transcript 35 during your re-examination, you said the following: "Captain Dragan arrived on his own in Benkovac. He appeared." Then later on at transcript 49 you said, quote, with respect to Mr. Simatovic and Golubic: "I would have [sic] certainly have heard about him establishing such a place." I'm going to ask that you now look at a short video clip of Captain Dragan himself describing how he came to this area and then I want to ask you whether you still maintain your position with respect to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that 2 -- Prosecution Exhibit 2976 be played for the witness. It is an excerpt from that video from 25 minutes, 30 seconds, until 26 minutes, 17 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness didn't testify over these three days about how Captain Dragan arrived. He's testifying about what Captain Dragan did when he arrived in Benkovac, how he got there, and who he tried to reach agreements with. Well, that's not something that the witness knows. I don't see how we can deal with anything that has to do with Captain Dragan before he arrived in Benkovac. What did the witness testify about with regard to the period prior to Dragan arriving in Benkovac? The witness has been testifying about Captain Dragan from the point in time when he arrived in Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the witness did testify that he came on his own, which is perhaps ambiguous language. Did you want to say, that he came on his own, that he came on his own initiative? Or I think even that ... but I have to check that carefully whether that is -- was what the evidence was, but, Mr. Groome --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's at transcript page 35, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 35. Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied, Mr. Petrovic. The answers, what happened upon arrival, do have some suggestive power as to under what circumstances and triggered by what he arrived, so therefore Mr. Groome is allowed to put this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Play the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask that excerpt from P2976, 25 minutes, 30 seconds, to 26 minutes, 17 seconds, be played now. Sir, I'd ask you to watch the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I think that I left a deep impression with them during that conversation. They asked me how and what I wanted to do. I told them what I wanted to do. They asked me how I was planning to do that. I told them everything about it. Then they asked me if I could put it down. Of course, I put it all down, a short 21-day course, roughly speaking. That is when I became friends with Frenki, in a way. It went much further than that official conversation. Regardless of this new friendship, the service is the service, and Frenki's order given at the Metropol was clear. "Captain Vasiljkovic: He said 'Sit and wait, and when it's time to go down there, we'll all go.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies, Your Honour. First of all, the witness could hear the anchor as well. There was a sentence by the narrator, not by Captain Dragan. That was one thing. Another thing is the context. When was this uttered and what period did it refer to? We can perhaps deduce it from the documentary, but the witness is unclear as to what period it refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, could you give the context to the witness to the extent needed to answer any question you may have in relation to this video?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This particular meeting that Captain Dragan is referring to is a meeting he had with Mr. Simatovic in the Metropol hotel with another operative form the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least what is said in this context.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I don't recall the exact date of that. I believe that it's in early 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, the witness being sufficiently informed about the context. Then please put your question to the witness, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So my question to you, DFS-014, is: Do you still maintain that Captain Dragan arrived in the Krajina on his own without any affiliation or relationship to any organisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What year do you have in mind? 1991, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you said he arrived on his own, what period were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in 1993 he appeared alone. I wasn't discussing who sent him or who he brought along. He didn't have a driver. I didn't mean to say that he came of his own accord. I was trying to say that he appeared there by himself, alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you do not know of whose accord he came there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who gave him authority or whether he needed any permission to come at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And secondly, you -- at T49, transcript 49 today, you were quite unequivocal when you said, with respect to Mr. Simatovic: "I would have [sic] certainly have heard about him establishing such a place." Hearing Captain Dragan's recounting of how he came to establish training centres in the Krajina, does this give you reason to reconsider how certain you are that you were well informed about Mr. Simatovic's role in the establishing of those training centres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't change my position much, because Defence counsel asked me if I -- whether I would have had knowledge if Frenki had managed or lead anything, so it entails a period of time. It wasn't done in a moment. Managing or leading takes time, especially on location in a camp or similar facility. That is what I meant. As for my position having seen this footage, it has not changed. I am aware of Captain Dragan's movements. I know he was an adventurer. And in the Krajina he attempted to command the Benkovac Brigade. And in 1995 he even wanted to command the whole army. In Serbia in 1999 and 2000 he ran for Serbian president. Who could trust such a man? I never trusted him, and that is why we were never on particularly good terms. He lacked my trust. I don't know what the statement is based on or where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My final question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My final question to you, sir, is: Prior to seeing this videotape, were you aware that Captain Dragan believed that Mr. Simatovic had given him an order with respect to the establishment of training centres in the Krajina? Were you aware of that before today?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, sorry, where do we find that in the footage, the part just quoted by my learned friend, and what year does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the year we have discussed, I think, a minute ago. We are talking about early 1991, isn't it, Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And let's just see the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The portion of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The portion of the video played --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Regardless --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- clearly -- clearly suggests that -- and I'm not saying whether that's true or not, but clearly suggests that the arrival of Captain Dragan was triggered by a meeting he had with Mr. Simatovic in which he was, at least, to say it, encouraged.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it says more than that, with all due respect. And if I can put to the witness exactly the portion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Captain Dragan says: "Regardless of this new friendship, the service is the service, and Frenki's order given at the Metropol was clear. He said 'Sit and wait, and when it's time to go down there, we'll all go.'" And my question to you is: Were you aware of that prior to today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one question for you. Well, I should be careful in saying one question, Mr. Petrovic. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You told us that you communicated with your superiors in Zagreb until the 5th of January, 1991, and you told us that they never cautioned me or they never gave you any information about Serbian MUP presence in the area. You remember giving that testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would have been a MUP presence in the Krajina area within your jurisdiction, would you consider that to be of such importance that they would or even should have told you about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If nothing else, they should at least have warned me of the importance of gathering additional information. They frequently asked me whether I could observe any influx of people from Serbia who hail from the Krajina, because there were suspicions that there were people from Serbia arriving in the Krajina to man the barricades. My personal observation, and by gathering information from the police, I could tell them that no such arrivals were registered or observed in terms of ordinary citizens who hail from the Krajina and came back from Serbia. For example, that is the kind of information the people in Zagreb always wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not asking about individual civilians, but I was talking about presence of persons linked to the MUP of Serbia. Would that have been information you would have expected them to convey to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DFS-014 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I should have been acquainted with that. Basically, first and foremost, to try to be careful so that no one would try to have me killed. It would have been of interest for me to know what else was going on in the Krajina without my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you also told us that when you heard from colleagues that Frenki was around, or MUP - you linked, apparently, Frenki to MUP - that you did not consider this worth to even verify. Why is it that before the 5th of January you considered this to be relevant information and why didn't you consider it relevant enough to pay further attention to when you heard that in the beginning of 1991 a MUP, Frenki, was present in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no further questions, Witness DFS-014 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness DFS-014, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming, especially for coming in a week which is not the most convenient week, but that is immediately after Orthodox Christmas. We highly appreciate that you are willing to come back at this point in time. I would like to thank you very much for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'd like to thank Your Honours for having enabled me to present my view of the situation in the period between 1990 and 1995 in order to assist to the extent possible to resolve this case in a just manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day. And since there are no witnesses further this week, we will resume at Tuesday, the 17th of January, 9.00 in the morning -- no, no, I'm sorry. At quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon in this same courtroom, II. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of January, 2012, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.13 p.m.,
